summary: The cluster is cheap: about 2.1 s wall in total; ExprSizeAndBudgetTest is the only notable cost (4.8 % of scalus-core CPU, almost all from the n = 100 000 T1/T2 loops, C21-5), and the two Benchmark-tagged sort suites still lower about 20 programs in their constructors on every CI run (C21-6). Budget comparison suites compare costs but often not results: DatumEqualityBudgetTest and EqualsDataVsTypedComparisonTest never check that the compared programs return the same answer, and two tests assert nothing (C21-7, C21-8, C21-13). CostingIntegerTest is a set of saturation examples that one BigInt-oracle property replaces, and reading it found a main-code defect: satMul(-1, Long.MinValue) does not saturate (C21-1). The dropList-09 cost path is simulated four times on top of its conformance case (C21-3), and a mis-named test duplicates another (C21-4). The BuiltinCostModel JSON writer, toJsonString and flattenCostModel have no test and no caller (C21-12).

bit sizes of unit, bool, integer, var, lambda, let, singleton list

behaviors.pass: CIP-153 Value builtins and T7 lowering
behaviors.name: builtin Value ops cheaper than portable SortedMap ops; prelude Value ops lower to builtins at PV11

findings.claim: By reading (not executed): satMul(-1, Long.MinValue) returns Long.MinValue instead of saturating to Long.MaxValue. r = -1 * MinValue wraps to MinValue, and the overflow check r / a == b evaluates MinValue / -1, which the JVM (JLS 15.17.2) also wraps to MinValue, so it equals b and the wrapped r is returned. The mirrored order satMul(Long.MinValue, -1) is caught (r / a = 1). No test uses -1 with MinValue in that order. Practical reach is low: it needs a negative coefficient times an already negatively saturated value.
findings.action: Main-code note: detect the case explicitly, e.g. use Math.multiplyHigh(a, b) != (r >> 63) as the overflow test, or special-case a == -1 && b == Long.MinValue. Test side: the property in C21-2 covers it with edge values in the generator; until the fix lands, add satMul(-1L, Long.MinValue) == Long.MaxValue as an expected-failure example.
findings.verification: The defect is real. CostModel.scala:59-66 computes r = -1 * MinValue, which wraps to MinValue. The check r / a = MinValue / -1 also wraps to MinValue (JLS 15.17.2; Scala.js and Native emulate the same) and equals b, so the code returns MinValue, not MaxValue. Reversing the order is safe: satMul(MinValue, -1) gives r/a = 1 != -1, so it saturates. The defect cannot be reached from cost evaluation. The buggy case needs the right operand b == Long.MinValue. Every `*` site puts a non-negative memory size or a non-negative product on the right (CostModel.scala:92, 109, 121 c11*(x*y), 130, 161, 184, 192, 275, 290). At line 102 the right operand (arg1-arg2).max(minimum) has non-negative args, so it is never below -MaxValue. Corrected claim: satMul(-1, Long.MinValue) returns MinValue (latent, not reachable from any current costing function). Fix it as hygiene (Math.multiplyHigh check or a special case), not as a costing bug.

findings.claim: The satPlus/satMinus/satMul example groups (10 tests) are instances of one oracle law: satOp(a, b) == clamp(BigInt(a) op BigInt(b)) into [Long.MinValue, Long.MaxValue]. 255-266 repeat lines 15-16 word for word. 'satMul: edge cases with large numbers' (175-191) asserts product2 > 0 || product2 == MaxValue, which no plausible mutation breaks. CostingInteger.fromBigInt (CostModel.scala:30-33) has no test (uncovered in the baseline).
findings.action: Replace 8-81, 167-191 and 255-266 with three forAll properties (shared, ScalaCheckPropertyChecks) against the BigInt clamp oracle, plus one for fromBigInt(x) == clamp(x). Use a Long generator that mixes Gen.oneOf(0, 1, -1, Long.MinValue, Long.MaxValue, MinValue+1, MaxValue-1, 3037000499L, 3037000500L) with Arbitrary[Long]. Keep the extension-operator tests 84-111 as one short example each.
findings.coverageRisk: low: every deleted example value is in the edge generator; the property will fail on C21-1 until that is fixed
findings.verification: The oracle law clamp(BigInt(a) op BigInt(b)) holds for satPlus (CostModel.scala:43-48), satMinus (51-56) and fromBigInt (30-33). It holds for satMul except the single pair (-1, MinValue) from C21-1. CostingIntegerTest.scala:255-266 repeat lines 15-16. Every deleted example value is in the proposed edge set or follows from it (for example (MaxValue-1)+1 checks the exact boundary at line 170). Two parts are wrong. (1) The claim that no mutation breaks 175-191 is false: 3037000500^2 = 9223372037000250000 > MaxValue. If the overflow check is removed, product2 wraps negative and the assert at 187-190 fails. That test is weak but not vacuous. (2) A random draw hits (-1, MinValue) about 1/81 of the times both operands come from the 9-value edge set. So the satMul property would fail intermittently, not always, until C21-1 is fixed. Corrected action: land the satMul fix before (or with) the property, or pin (-1, MinValue) as an explicit example. Then replace 8-81, 167-191 and 255-266 with the clamp-oracle properties as proposed.

findings.claim: Four tests simulate the dropList-09 cost path with the same numbers (intercept 116711, slope 1957, arg Long.MaxValue): CostingIntegerTest 113-131, 148-165 (same arithmetic through satMul/satPlus), 210-228 (LinearInX, a subset of 230-253) and CostingIntegerJVMTest (with four println calls). The conformance case dropList-09 already pins the end-to-end result cpu 9223372036854775807, mem 704.
findings.action: Delete CostingIntegerJVMTest.scala, and CostingIntegerTest 148-165 and 210-228. Keep 113-131 and 230-253 (they also check ConstantCost memory). Move the one fromInputStream call into the C21-12 roundtrip test so that API keeps a caller.
findings.coverageRisk: low: BuiltinCostModel.fromInputStream (a one-line read wrapper) loses its only test unless C21-12 picks it up; the saturation logic stays covered by 113-131, 230-253 and dropList-09 conformance
findings.verification: 148-165 runs the same arithmetic as 113-131: the `*`/`+` extensions inline to satMul/satPlus (CostModel.scala:72-73) with the same numbers (116711, 1957, MaxValue). 210-228 (LinearInX, arg2=1) is a subset of 230-253 (LinearInX plus ConstantCost mem, arg2=704). CostingIntegerJVMTest.scala:8-45 asserts three things. (a) The dropList entry in the loaded model is non-null. (b) memoryUsageLiteral(10^19) == MaxValue. (c) cpu == MaxValue. The conformance case dropList-09 (budget.expected cpu 9223372036854775807) covers (b) and (c) end to end. If memoryUsageLiteral did not saturate, the cpu would be finite. PlutusConformanceTest.scala:262-291 checks the budget. It runs in the JVM, JS and Native subclasses, and none of them ignores dropList. It uses builtinCostModelE.json, whose dropList coefficients (E json:1217-1218) equal C json:414-415. Caveat: CostingIntegerJVMTest is the only code that parses builtinCostModelC.json and the only caller of fromInputStream (grep). So delete it only together with the C21-12 roundtrip test that loads builtinCostModelC.json through fromInputStream, as the action already says.

findings.claim: Test 68-74 is named 'List.cons(true, Nil) size is 63' but its body compiles List.singleton(true), the same body as 76-80. The prelude List has no `cons` method, so the name describes nothing.
findings.coverageRisk: none: the body is identical to 76-80
findings.verification: ExprSizeAndBudgetTest.scala:68-74, test 'List.cons(true, Nil) size is 63', has the body compile(plutus.prelude.List.singleton(true)).toUplcOptimized() with assert bitSize == 63. Lines 76-80 have the same body and the same assertion. The real Cons constructor case is covered separately at 59-66 and stays. Deleting 68-74 loses nothing.

findings.claim: ExprSizeAndBudgetTest is 4.8 % of scalus-core test CPU and 0.92 s wall; 0.91 s of it are the three T1/T2 proofs, which run CEK loops of n = 100 000 for both encodings to amortize the one-off entry cost. The T1 test already shows the exact method: differencing two loop lengths cancels the entry cost, because cost is linear in n.
findings.action: In both T2 tests and in T1, measure at n1 = 10 and n2 = 1010 and assert ((z2 - s2) - (z1 - s1)) / (n2 - n1) == 96000 cpu and 600 mem. Keep the n = 0, 10, 1000 loop of the countdown test.
findings.coverageRisk: none: the per-call constant is exact under differencing; the same assertions remain

findings.claim: Both suites are tagged Benchmark and excluded with '-l', but ScalaTest still instantiates excluded suites to read their tags. Their `candidates` (14 and 5 programs) and `isSortedTerm` are strict vals, so every CI run lowers and optimizes about 20 sort programs (initSupportBindings plus V3Optimizer each, see F-14) that no test uses. timings.csv shows 0.0 s for both because constructor time is not attributed to a test; the cost is an estimate.
findings.action: Make `candidates` and `isSortedTerm` lazy vals in both suites (the matrix is already lazy).

findings.claim: The test compares budgets of two programs but never checks what they return. evaluateDebug.budget is also defined for a failed run, so a regression that makes `hasInlineDatum` return false early, or fail, makes the 'wrap' side cheaper and the test still passes.
findings.action: Evaluate with evaluateDebug.success (or match Result.Success) and assert both results are (con bool True); add one case where the output datum differs (count 43) and assert both return False.

findings.claim: No test in the file checks that the `===` program and the equalsData program return the same boolean; only budgets are compared, and a failed run also has a budget. A lowering bug that makes `===` return the wrong answer, or fail fast, would make it 'cheaper' and pass. 'pack+equalsData vs Case+equalsInteger' (292-335) has no assertion at all; it only logs.
findings.action: In every example and forAll test, assert both programs succeed with the same result (the forAll ones give an oracle: result == (a == b)). In 292-335 assert both return True and the ordering that the comment claims, or delete the test as a report.

findings.claim: The forAll tests draw a and b independently, so they almost never produce equal values, and `===`/equalsData stop at the first differing field. The full-traversal path (the worst case a validator pays) is checked only by the example tests for TxOutRef (126-145), Address (147-166) and OutputDatum (168-184), each with one fixed equal value. Those examples are instances of the forAll properties at 416-468 once the generator also yields equal pairs.
findings.action: Generate pairs with Gen.oneOf(arbitrary.map(a => (a, a)), independent pair) in the TxOutRef, Address and OutputDatum properties (and the tuple ones). Then delete the three example tests 126-184.
findings.coverageRisk: low: the fixed values (32-byte TxId, PubKeyCredential without stake, NoOutputDatum) are within the generators' range; verify the Address generator also yields the no-stake shape
findings.verification: The fixed example values are in the generators' range. TxId is genByteStringOfN(32) (v3 ArbitraryInstances.scala:12), and the TxOutRef index includes 0. Address is autoDerived (v1:53), with PubKeyCredential (v1:43) and an arbitrary prelude Option that includes None (uplc/test/ArbitraryInstances.scala:366). OutputDatum includes NoOutputDatum (v2:15). The properties at EqualsDataVsTypedComparisonTest.scala:416-468 assert the same relations as the examples at 126-184 (steps <, memory >, fee <; equality for OutputDatum). Independent pairs mostly differ early, as the report says. The weak point: nobody has checked that the relations hold for every full-traversal equal pair, for example Address with Some(StakingHash(ScriptCredential)) or a large TxOutRef index. The examples show only one shape each. Corrected action: add the equal-pair branch to the generators and run the properties. Delete the examples 126-184 only if the extended properties pass. If they fail, record that as a finding about the === vs equalsData cost claim, not as a reason to keep the examples silently.

findings.claim: `PlutusV3.compile { (d1: Data, d2: Data) => equalsData(d1, d2) }` is written 13 times, and the 9 example tests repeat the same 8 lines (two budgets, two sizes, two info lines) around 3 assertions.
findings.action: Compile eqData once as a private val. Add a local helper compare(labelA, progA, labelB, progB, args: Data*): (ExUnits, ExUnits) that evaluates, checks the results (C21-8) and logs formatLine. Each example test becomes 3-5 lines.

findings.claim: The six fee-pin tests 108-221 copy the same bs1..bs5 setup and the same 4 assertions; they differ only in the compiled accessor, the argument and the pinned numbers. Dead code: `ifBudget0` (85) is never read, `params` (96) shadows the class val, the `iterations` parameter of compareEncodings (277) is never used, and the comment at 30 names SimpleSirToUplcLowering while the code uses ScottEncodingLowering.
findings.action: Turn 108-221 into one table (name, compiled fn, arg Data, expected term, mem, cpu, fee) with a loop of test(...) registrations. Remove ifBudget0, the inner params val and the iterations parameter (and its 4 call-site arguments); fix the comment.

findings.claim: The writer half of the BuiltinCostModel and cost-function ReadWriters, toJsonString and flattenCostModel are public and fully uncovered in the baseline; nothing in the repository calls them. Only the reader half is exercised (reference models, fromInputStream).
findings.action: Add a shared roundtrip test: for vanRossemReferenceD and vanRossemReferenceE (and the model from builtinCostModelC.json via fromInputStream), assert fromJsonString(m.toJsonString) == m, and that flattenCostModel has one entry per non-null cost parameter with the expected key for one known parameter (e.g. 'addInteger-cpu-arguments-intercept').

findings.claim: 'UplcConstr and Data-packed paths stay within sight of each other' is documented as a regression guard ('a large divergence would mean the UplcConstr lowering had drifted') but asserts nothing; it only logs. 'report: cost by shape at n=32' also only logs and repeats evaluations that 110-120 already run.
findings.action: In 144-162 assert a loose bound on the ratio per row (e.g. 0.5 <= dataCost / constr <= 2). Fold the n=32 cost log of 122-128 into the 110-120 loop as info lines and delete 122-128.
findings.coverageRisk: none: adds an assertion; the report output is kept

findings.claim: Comments still describe the deleted UplcConstrListOperations.sort intrinsic as live: sortDataPacked 'runs the PRELUDE sort body rather than the intrinsic' (51-57), Box 'dispatches to UplcConstrListOperations.sort' (168-170), sortPlain likewise (182-184), and 130-139 is a stale scaladoc directly followed by a second one (140-143), so only the second attaches to the test. The class scaladoc (15-20) says the intrinsic was deleted.
findings.action: Delete the stale doc comment 130-139 and rewrite 51-57, 168-170 and 182-184 to say both paths run the prelude sort.

findings.claim: The same input shapes (random with seed 42, ascending, descending, allEqual, fewUnique, organPipe; SortBudgetTest adds sawtooth) are written three times with identical expressions.
findings.action: Extract an object SortInputShapes (scalus-core/jvm test, package scalus.uplc.eval) with `all: Seq[(String, Int => Seq[BigInt])]` and use it in the three suites (UplcConstrSortTest maps it to its Int => Seq form).

findings.claim: The optimizeUplc=false test re-writes 8 of the compile {} blocks from `candidates` only to lower them with other Options, and labels the preludeSort program 'OLDUNUSED' (213) although it is the shipped NEW(prelude) sort.
findings.action: Keep a lazy Seq of (name, SIR) from compile {} and derive both term lists with .toUplc() and .toUplc(using unoptimized)(); rename the label to NEW(prelude).

findings.claim: The three 'BuiltinCostModel from ... Protocol Parameters' tests repeat the same 12-line body (load JSON, three fromSeq, three fromPlutusParams) and differ only in loader, file and expected sizes/values.
findings.action: Extract a local helper load(pparams): (Seq v1, v2, v3, params V1..V3) that also builds the three models, and keep the per-file assertions in each test.

verification: Verify agent, read-only, 2026-10-22: 5 findings of scope merge-duplicate-tests, to-property or main-bug; 2 confirmed, 3 narrowed, 0 disproved and dropped [P2-12]. Other findings are unverified.
